newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan jewellers face crisis as retailer goes bust.
newsitem.headline: Japan jewellers face crisis as retailer goes bust.

text.p: The bankruptcy of a big Japanese jeweller has sent shock waves through an already embattled sector and may spur trade houses and other firms to scale back or withdraw from the business, industry sources say.
Flagging sales, stepped-up competition from imported jewellery and the fragmented, inefficient structure of the industry point to a painful period of restructuring and consolidation ahead, they say.

A Japanese district court last week declared that Yokohama-based jewellery retailer Coco Yamaoka Hoshokuten and two of its affiliates were bankrupt, with debts totalling 60 billion yen ($512 million), the largest ever amassed by a Japanese jeweller.
Industry sources also said Coco was the largest Japanese retailer ever to be forced into bankruptcy.
While several jewellery manufacturers and wholesalers have gone bust in recent months, bankruptcies among retailers have been relatively rare.
"(Coco's) bankruptcy will have a huge effect on the domestic jewellery market," said Yukuji Sonoda, president of Sumisho Gold Corp.

"Not only is it inevitable that some related jewellery firms (that did business with Coco) will collapse, but the bankruptcy could force trade houses to withdraw from the jewellery business altogether," he said.

Many trade houses lend precious metals to jewellery manufacturers or offer them other forms of credit, and they may cut back or discontinue such transactions as jewellery firms' credit risk increases. This in turn would make it harder for small jewellery firms to stay in business, sources said.
Coco Yamaoka, which specialised in diamond jewellery, had 112 shops nationwide and ranked sixth among Japan's jewellery retailers, said Teikoku Databank, a private credit research company.

Of the 60 billion yen ($512 million) in debts held by Coco and two affiliates, six billion to 10 billion yen ($51.2 million to $85.4 million) was believed to be with other jewellery firms and precious metal traders, including leading Japanese trade houses Marubeni Corp and Itochu Corp, several sources said.
A Marubeni spokesman said the trade house had no direct dealings with Coco Yamaoka, although he declined to comment on whether there were any transactions with Coco's affiliates.
A spokesman for Itochu was not immediately available for comment.

Industry observers said a slump in jewellery sales after the collapse of Japan's so-called "bubble economy" in the late 1980s, combined with rising pressure from imports, suggested that the rise in bankruptcies would continue.
"The trend towards rising jewellery imports and falling domestic production was particularly evident last year," said Sumisho Gold's Sonoda.
"(Coco's) collapse will accelerate the industry's hollowing out, as Hong Kong-made jewellery could take away most of the domestic share of Japan-made non-brand jewellery," he said.

Teikoku Databank calculated that 42 jewellery firms with debts of 15.22 billion yen ($130 million) went bankrupt in October and November last year, up from 28 firms with 8.17 billion yen ($69.8 million) in debts during the same two months the year before.
Industry sources said more consolidation would be needed.

"Currently, there are about 4,000 jewellery firms, including retailers and wholesalers, in Japan. But the number is too many considering the market has contracted gradually since the end of the bubble," a senior official at a large bullion house said. He said the number of firms would have to fall by at least half in order for the industry to revive.
The sources said lax management and complex, often circuitous distribution routes were also to blame for the industry's woes. ---Tokyo Commodity Desk, +81-3-3432-7431
